question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Christian Missionary Centres and their founding orders in India]
options: Goa — Franciscan missionaries arrived first in 1500
Madurai — Roberto de Nobili established Jesuit mission in 1606
Serampore — William Carey founded the Baptist Mission in 1800
Tranquebar — Portuguese Jesuits established the first mission in 1706
wrong_fact: The Tranquebar mission (1706) was founded by Danish-Halle missionaries Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau — NOT by Portuguese Jesuits. It was a Lutheran/Protestant mission under Danish patronage.
explanation: Goa saw Franciscans arrive with Cabral's fleet in 1500, making it correct. Roberto de Nobili correctly established his inculturation Jesuit mission in Madurai in 1606. William Carey did found the Serampore Mission (Baptist Missionary Society) in 1800. Tranquebar, however, was the site of the first Protestant mission in India, started by German Lutheran missionaries Ziegenbalg and Plütschau under Danish royal patronage — not Portuguese Jesuits.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Missionary and region of primary activity in colonial India]
options: Francis Xavier — Goa and coastal South India (1542–1552)
Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg — Tranquebar, Tamil Nadu from 1706
Robert de Nobili — Bombay (Salsette Island) from 1606
wrong_fact: Robert de Nobili worked in Madurai (Tamil Nadu), not Bombay/Salsette Island. He adopted Tamil Brahmin customs to spread Christianity in the Madurai Nayak kingdom.
explanation: Francis Xavier's mission across Goa and coastal South India (1542–52) is well documented. Alexander Duff pioneered English-medium missionary education in Calcutta after 1830. Ziegenbalg's Tranquebar base is historically accurate. However, Robert de Nobili's famous inculturation experiment was conducted in Madurai, not Bombay — he dressed as a Brahmin sannyasi to reach upper-caste Hindus in the Deccan South, far from the Konkan coast.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Missionary institution and its location/significance in colonial India]
options: Serampore College (1818) — Serampore, Bengal; first degree-granting institution in Asia
St. Thomas College, Palayamkottai (1896) — Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu; oldest degree college in southern India
Wilson College (1832) — Bombay; founded by John Wilson of the Scottish Missionary Society
Hislop College (1853) — Nagpur; founded by Stephen Hislop of the Free Church of Scotland
wrong_fact: St. Thomas College, Palayamkottai was founded in 1896 but the claim of 'oldest degree college in southern India' is incorrect. Serampore College (1818) and other institutions predate it. The claim of oldest is sometimes made for the Madras Christian College (founded 1837 as a high school, degree college 1877).
explanation: Serampore College founded by Carey, Marshman and Ward in 1818 was indeed chartered as Asia's first degree-granting institution. Wilson College, Bombay (1832) was correctly founded by John Wilson. Hislop College, Nagpur (1853) was indeed founded by Stephen Hislop of the Free Church of Scotland. The incorrect option is about St. Thomas College, Palayamkottai — the 'oldest degree college in southern India' claim is historically contested and the date/distinction misrepresents its actual historical standing relative to Madras Christian College (1877 as degree college).
